title: DfE Decoded #170: Elective Home Education, Choice Should Never Mean Invisibility
author: Paul Urry
summary: Urry reads the DfE consultation on elective home education guidance and argues that EHE should neither trigger suspicion nor switch off safeguarding curiosity. He sets parents' right against local authorities' duty and asks how an education that cannot be seen can be judged suitable. He notes that school provides informal visibility, that unmet SEND and attendance breakdown often sit beneath 'elective' decisions, and that schools must never nudge families toward EHE. His practical proposals for school leaders are to treat deregistration as a transition, to ask five safeguarding questions before a child leaves, and to hold multi-agency conversations for complex cases. He concludes that guidance alone cannot fix what is really a legal gap.
points: School supplies hundreds of small moments of adult visibility, so leaving roll removes a protective layer even when home education is a good choice.
Many 'elective' choices follow unmet SEND, attendance breakdown or conflict with school, so schools should ask why now without interrogating.
Schools must never present EHE as the easy answer to a difficult pupil, which becomes off-rolling by suggestion.
Without longitudinal data on who leaves and what happens next, thriving home education cannot be distinguished from educational disappearance.
quotes: EHE should never automatically trigger suspicion. But neither should the label EHE automatically switch off professional curiosity.
School is not simply somewhere children receive lessons. It is also somewhere they are seen.
That does not mean EHE makes children unsafe. It means we have removed one important protective layer.
The wording may sound innocent. The power relationship is not.
A statutory power is only protective if it can operate quickly enough to protect the child.
Without longitudinal information, we cannot properly distinguish thriving home education from educational disappearance.
Because elective home education should mean choosing a different way to educate a child. It should never become a way for that child to disappear from education altogether.
